title: British silver hallmark date letters: London, Birmingham, Sheffield, Chester
applies_to: Date letters on British hallmarked silver (also gold, where the same letter was used) from the London (1678-2000), Birmingham (1773-2000), Sheffield (1773-2000) and Chester (1701-1962) assay offices. Identify the office from the town mark first, then match the letter's case and style within that office. Edinburgh, Glasgow and Dublin are not covered.

row_fields.style: roman | gothic (black letter / Old English) | court_hand | italic | script | block
row_fields.year: first calendar year of the assay year (from 1975, the calendar year)
row_fields.cycle_start: first year of the cycle this letter belongs to
row_fields.style_basis: label = style named in Chaffers/Jackson; glyph = read from published letterforms
row_fields.alt_year / alt_year_source: year given by a disagreeing source
row_fields.confidence: present only when low or disputed
row_fields.sources: source keys that support the row

sources.name: BullionByPost (Birmingham bullion dealer): Hallmark date letters 1900-2019, chart image for Birmingham, Edinburgh, London, Sheffield, Dublin, Chester and Glasgow
sources.notes: Added as an independent third source for the cycles after 1924, which Jackson (1921) and Chaffers (1924) predate, so that no row rests on silvermakersmarks and SilverMine alone. Chart image: media.bullionbypost.co.uk/media/uploads/pages/images/2019/07/05/Hallmark_years.jpg. Read year by year on 2026-11-22 against every row from 1925 to 2000 (London 1936-2000, Birmingham 1925-2000, Sheffield 1943-2000, Chester 1926-1962): all 236 agree on year and style. Its I/J glyphs were not read closely enough to settle the letter: Chester 1934 (black letter, could be I or J), Birmingham 1958 (italic) and 1983 (script); Birmingham Assay Office's own archive later settled 1958 and 1983 as J. Not used for rows before 1925.

sources.name: Birmingham Assay Office: date letter archive (every date letter struck at Birmingham since 1773, with images)
sources.notes: The office's own record of its punches (paid access, bought by Joe on 2026-11-22). Read caption by caption for 1773-2000 and compared with every Birmingham row: 224 of 228 agree. 1787 P is not in the archive. 1832, 1958 and 1983 are captioned J (the images show a descender) where the earlier sources read I; those rows now carry J, with the earlier reading in 'note'. From 1975 the letter is shared, so 1983 J applies at every office. The images are the office's copyright and are not reproduced.

sources.name: Checked and not used: 925-1000.com; theassayoffice.co.uk date-letter archive; antiquejewellers.com charts
sources.notes: 925-1000.com sits behind a Cloudflare bot check, which was not bypassed. The Birmingham Assay Office archive is paywalled. antiquejewellers.com has text charts, but they are wrong for several cycles (e.g. London 1756-75 given as Roman capitals, 1916-35 as capitals, 1936-55 as lower case; Birmingham cases wrong), so they were rejected.

caveats: Until 1974 a date letter covers an assay year, not a calendar year. 'year' is the first calendar year of that assay year and 'year_label' gives the span (London 's' of 1753 = 29/30 May 1753 to May 1754). The letter changed about 29 May in London and in July at Birmingham, Sheffield and Chester (5 August at Chester 1839-1889). From 1975 it changes on 1 January everywhere.

The same letter in the same case recurs in several cycles of one office. For example, London Roman lower case was used in 1736-55, 1776-95, 1816-35 and 1896-1915. So case, style, shield shape and the other marks (see rules) must all agree before a row is used. Shield shapes are not in this table.

'style' uses short descriptors: gothic = black letter / Old English; court_hand; roman; italic; script; block = plain sans-serif capitals (Sheffield 1868-92). style_basis 'label' means Chaffers or Jackson names the style in the cycle heading. 'glyph' means no textual label was found, so the style was read from the letterforms in silvermakersmarks and the SilverMine charts, which agree. This applies to all post-1924 cycles and some Chester cycles.

Court-hand (London 1697-1715) and black-letter capitals and small letters are hard to tell apart by case. London court hand is recorded as lower case by convention. The 1697 Goldsmiths' minute calls the first letter 'a great Court A' (McKinley).

London 1697 has two rows: 'a' (27 Mar-28 May 1697, rare, the first Britannia-standard letter) and 'b' (1697-98). London 1696 't' was used only until 27 Mar 1697. London 1735 is printed as a Roman 'V' (the 20th letter of that cycle), not U.
Chester 1726-1750 (script capitals): Jackson 1921 and silvermakersmarks agree. Chaffers 1924 adds a script J at 1735-36 and so dates K-Z one year later (given as alt_year).

Chester 1751-1775 is low confidence. Jackson 1921 prints several letters as 'B or b', 'D or d' and so on ('case': 'either'). Chaffers 1924 starts the cycle in 1752-53 with capitals and a J (its years are given as alt_year). For U-Z (1770-1775) the sources disagree outright: rows are marked 'disputed' and carry the silvermakersmarks year with Jackson's in alt_year. Do not state these years with confidence.
Chester 1821: 'D' was used from 8 Nov 1821 to 5 Jul 1823. There is no 1822 letter; this is a real gap, not a missing row.

Sheffield 1773-1823 letters are in no alphabetical order and mix black-letter capitals, black-letter small letters (1785 y, 1786 k, 1792-95 u o m q) and Roman capitals (1796-98 Z X V). T appears for both 1780 and 1787: 1787 has the sovereign's-head duty mark and 1780 does not. X appears for both 1797 and 1817: 1817 has the crown struck upside down. E appears for 1773 (black letter) and 1799 (Roman).
Sheffield 1782: silvermakersmarks labels it C, but the black-letter glyph in both Jackson 1921 and silvermakersmarks looks like a G. It is kept as C with a note.
From 1780 to 1853 Sheffield small articles often carry the crown and date letter in one punch (crown above, later beside, the letter). The date letter is still the same letter.

1975-1999 and 2000 rows are repeated for London, Birmingham and Sheffield because the letter was shared by all offices (Edinburgh too). In 1975-1999 the ninth letter, 1983, is a script J in Birmingham Assay Office's own archive (earlier sources read it as I). 2001-2024 (lower case, per silvermakersmarks with i omitted so 2008 = j) and the 2025 cycle (from 'A') are left out: only one reliable source gives the letters year by year.

Not covered: Edinburgh, Glasgow and Dublin (skipped rather than guessed; their cycles have irregular years and duplicate letters that could not be cross-checked in the time available), and the closed offices of Exeter, Newcastle, York and Norwich. Birmingham and Sheffield opened in 1773; Chester's table starts with the 1701 statutory cycle and ends when the office closed on 24 Aug 1962.
Gold wares, watch cases and imported wares can carry different punches and shield shapes from those described here (Boettcher). Watch cases were exempt from the duty mark from 1798.

Several reference books, and some online charts, disagree on individual letters. antiquejewellers.com was checked and rejected because it is wrong on whole cycles. When a mark does not match a row exactly (style or case), the app should say the year is uncertain rather than pick the nearest row.

rules.fact: From 27 Mar 1697 the Britannia standard (95.8% silver) was compulsory. Its marks are the figure of Britannia and a lion's head erased, in place of the lion passant and leopard's head. Sterling was allowed again from 1 Jun 1720, and Britannia stayed optional afterwards. From 1697 to 1701 only London could assay; Chester used Britannia marks 1701-1719/20.
rules.narrows: Britannia plus lion's head erased with a London letter means 1697-1720 (or a later optional Britannia piece). A sterling lion with a London letter from the 1697-1715 court-hand cycle is not expected.

rules.fact: In the Britannia period, makers' marks were the first two letters of the surname (Chaffers). In 1739 makers had to replace their punches with their initials, and new punches were used from 19 Jul 1739 (silvermakersmarks, London 'd' of 1739).
rules.narrows: A two-letter surname mark suggests 1697 to c.1739. Initials of Christian name and surname suggest after 1739 (or before 1697).

rules.fact: A sovereign's-head mark showed that plate duty had been paid. London struck it from 1 Dec 1784 (letter 'i' of 1784-85). At first the head was incuse (sunk), on letters i 1784-85 and k 1785-86, and it faced the other way from 1786. The duty was abolished in 1890: London dropped the head from 2 May 1890 (during 'O' 1889-90), and Birmingham from 2 May 1890 (during 'p').
rules.narrows: A head present means 1784-1890. It is absent before Dec 1784 and after May 1890. Whose head it is (George III, George IV, William IV, Victoria) narrows further, but new heads were often introduced some years after a new reign.

rules.fact: An incuse standing-Britannia 'drawback' mark was struck on exported wares when the duty was refunded, from 1 Dec 1784 to 24 Jul 1785 (silvermakersmarks). The Goldsmiths' Company says it was withdrawn in July 1785.
rules.narrows: An incuse Britannia with sterling marks means 1784-85.

rules.fact: When the duty was doubled in 1797, doubled or notched duty-head punches were used: London 6 Jul 1797-28 May 1798 (letter B), Sheffield from 15 Jul 1797 for about 9 months (letter X).
rules.narrows: A doubled duty head points to 1797-98.

rules.fact: Watch cases were exempt from duty from March 1798, so watch cases hallmarked after the 1797-98 assay year have no sovereign's head.
rules.narrows: Do not use a missing duty head to date a watch case to before 1784 or after 1890.

rules.fact: The London leopard's head was crowned until 1821 and uncrowned afterwards. The change happened during the 1821-22 assay year: both punch forms occur with letter 'f' (silvermakersmarks). Jackson dates it 1821 and the Goldsmiths' Company 1822. Chaffers 1924 says 'after 1823' (conflict). The head was also absent from 27 Mar 1697 to 1720 on Britannia-standard plate.
rules.narrows: Crowned means 1821-22 'f' or earlier. Uncrowned with a date letter means 1821-22 'f' or later.

rules.fact: The London sterling lion was passant guardant (head turned to face the viewer) from 1544 until 1821. From the 1821-22 punches onward it is lion passant, with the head in profile facing the direction of travel.
rules.narrows: A guardant lion with a London letter means 1821-22 or earlier. A profile lion means 1821-22 or later.

rules.fact: Birmingham's lion was passant guardant until 1875 and passant afterwards. Chester's was passant guardant until 1822, passant 1823-1883, then guardant again from 1884 until 1962.
rules.narrows: Separates Chester 1823-1883 from other Chester cycles, and Birmingham before and after 1875.

rules.fact: London: leopard's head (crowned to 1821, uncrowned after; replaced by a lion's head erased on Britannia-standard plate). Birmingham: anchor, from 31 Aug 1773, unchanged. Sheffield: crown for silver from 1773; a rose from 1975, per silvermakersmarks and the SilverMine chart, which shows the rose with the 1975 'A'. Wikipedia says the rose came in 1977 (conflict). Chester: the city arms. Chaffers says the arms changed about 1720 to three demi-lions dimidiated with three half-garbs. Later Chester marks (e.g. 1938) show a sword between three wheatsheaves. Chester also struck a leopard's head with its marks until 1838-39: Jackson Tables II-VII include it, and Table VIII from 1839-40 does not.
rules.narrows: Identifies the office. A Chester mark with a leopard's head is 1838-39 or earlier, which separates Chester script 1726-50 from script 1901-25 (silvermakersmarks makes the same point).

rules.fact: On small articles the Sheffield crown and date letter were often struck in one punch, from 1780 to 1853: crown above the letter until about 1828, beside it afterwards.
rules.narrows: A crown-and-letter combined punch means Sheffield 1780-1853.

rules.fact: From 1815 to 1819 the Sheffield crown is found struck upside down (Jackson). silvermakersmarks notes inverted-crown variants in 1815.
rules.narrows: Separates Sheffield X of 1817 (inverted crown) from X of 1797.

rules.fact: London changed its letter on 19 May (St Dunstan's day) until 1660 and on about 29 May from the early 1700s to 1974. Birmingham changed in July. Sheffield changed in July (the first Monday in July per silvermakersmarks). Chester changed about 5 July until 1839, 5 August 1839-1889, and 1 July from 1890. All offices change on 1 January from 1975.
rules.narrows: Turns a letter into calendar months (see year_label).

rules.fact: The Hallmarking Act 1973 came into force on 2 Jan 1975. From then all remaining offices use the same date letter, changing each 1 January: 1975 is script capital A and J is not used. The old cycles were cut short: London italic a-t ended at t (1974) and Sheffield italic A-G ended at G (1974). The Act also introduced platinum marks.
rules.narrows: A letter from 1975 on dates the item to one calendar year, whichever office struck it.

rules.fact: From 1 Jan 1999 a numeric fineness mark (e.g. 925) is compulsory. The date letter and the traditional lion passant became optional, so a modern piece may have no date letter.
rules.narrows: A 925 mark with no date letter is consistent with 1999 or later.

rules.fact: Optional commemorative marks: George V Silver Jubilee (twin heads), 1934-35, with London letters t and u (Birmingham from Feb 1934). Elizabeth II Coronation, 1953-54, with London R (1952-53) and S (1953-54). Silver Jubilee 1977 (C). Millennium mark 1999 and 2000. Also Golden Jubilee 2002, Diamond Jubilee 2012, Platinum Jubilee 2022 and the Charles III Coronation 2023.
rules.narrows: A commemorative mark pins the year to those listed.

rules.fact: From 1867 imported plate was additionally struck with an 'F' in an oval. From 1904 imported wares received separate import assay-office marks instead of the usual town marks.
rules.narrows: An 'F' in an oval means imported, 1867 or later. A foreign-ware office mark means imported, 1904 or later: do not read it as British-made.

rules.fact: Birmingham and Sheffield offices were founded by the Act of 1773 (Birmingham opened 31 Aug 1773; Sheffield's first piece was 20 Sep 1773). Chester was re-established as a statutory office in 1701 and closed on 24 Aug 1962.
rules.narrows: No Birmingham or Sheffield letters before 1773; no Chester letters after 1962.
